stem: Sikh tradition credits which Guru with shaping and settling the Gurmukhi script in which the Gurus' hymns are written?
options: Guru Angad, the second Guru
Guru Amar Das, the third Guru
Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru
Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru
why: Sikh tradition holds that Guru Angad, the second Guru, gave the Gurmukhi letters their settled form so Guru Nanak's hymns could be written down; Guru Arjan later compiled the Adi Granth in that script.
source: Sikh tradition (Guru Angad); Gurmukhi painti alphabet

es.stem: La tradición sij atribuye a ¿qué Guru haber dado forma y fijado la escritura gurmukhi, en la que están escritos los himnos de los Gurus?
options: Guru Angad, el segundo Guru
Guru Amar Das, el tercer Guru
Guru Ram Das, el cuarto Guru
Guru Arjan, el quinto Guru
es.why: La tradición sij sostiene que Guru Angad, el segundo Guru, dio a las letras gurmukhi su forma fija para que los himnos de Guru Nanak pudieran escribirse; más tarde Guru Arjan compiló el Adi Granth en esa escritura.

stem: In the Mool Mantar, the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib (Ang 1), what does the word nirbhau mean?
options: without enmity
self-existent
without fear
beyond time
why: Nirbhau is nir, without, plus bhau, fear: the One is without fear. Its neighbours in the Mool Mantar are nirvair (without enmity), akal murat (form beyond time) and saibhang (self-existent).

es.stem: En el Mool Mantar, las líneas con que abre el Guru Granth Sahib (Ang 1), ¿qué significa la palabra nirbhau?
options: sin enemistad
existente por sí mismo
sin temor alguno
más allá del tiempo
es.why: Nirbhau es nir, sin, más bhau, miedo: el Uno no tiene miedo. Sus vecinas en el Mool Mantar son nirvair (sin enemistad), akal murat (forma más allá del tiempo) y saibhang (existente por sí).

stem: In the first pauri of Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1), how does Guru Nanak say one becomes truthful (sachiaara) and the wall of falsehood is torn down?
options: by thinking it over a hundred thousand times
by keeping outward silence for endless hours
by walking in the hukam, the divine will
by piling up the goods of all the worlds
why: Pauri 1 says thought, silence, possessions and cleverness all fall short, then asks how to become true and answers: hukam rajaaee chalnaa, walk in the order of the One whose will it is, as written with us.
source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Japji Sahib, pauri 1)

es.stem: En la primera pauri del Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1), ¿cómo dice Guru Nanak que uno se vuelve veraz (sachiaara) y se derriba el muro de la falsedad?
options: pensándolo cien mil veces sin descanso
guardando silencio exterior horas sin fin
caminando en el hukam, la voluntad divina
acumulando los bienes de todos los mundos
es.why: La pauri 1 dice que el pensamiento, el silencio, las posesiones y la astucia no bastan; luego pregunta cómo volverse veraz y responde: hukam rajaaee chalnaa, caminar en el orden de Aquel cuya voluntad es, escrito junto con nosotros.

stem: In Pauri 16 of Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3), what does Guru Nanak say the mythic bull (dhaul) holding up the earth really is?
options: seva, selfless service, the child of true humility
dharam, right living, the child of compassion
naam, the Name, the child of the true Guru
hukam, the order, the child of the Creator
why: Pauri 16: dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot, the bull is dharma, son of compassion, held in place by contentment. Guru Nanak asks what would hold up a literal bull, since beyond this earth are more earths.
source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3 (Japji Sahib, pauri 16)

es.stem: En la pauri 16 del Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3), ¿qué dice Guru Nanak que es en verdad el toro mítico (dhaul) que sostiene la tierra?
options: seva, el servicio desinteresado, hijo de la humildad
dharam, la vida recta, hijo de la compasión
naam, el Nombre, hijo del verdadero Guru
hukam, el orden, hijo del Creador
es.why: Pauri 16: dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot, el toro es el dharma, hijo de la compasión, sostenido por el contentamiento. Guru Nanak pregunta qué sostendría a un toro literal, si más allá de esta tierra hay más tierras.

stem: Someone reads Pauri 28 of Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6), with its yogi's earrings, begging bag and ashes. What does Guru Nanak do with those items there?
options: requires Sikhs to wear them at the dawn prayer
allows them only for Sikhs who leave their homes
lists them as the dress of the five beloved ones
makes each an inner virtue, like contentment
why: Pauri 28 says: make contentment your earrings, modesty your begging bag, meditation your ashes, and humanity your order; conquer the mind and you conquer the world. The Gurus lived as householders.
source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6 (Japji Sahib, pauri 28)

es.stem: Alguien lee la pauri 28 del Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6), con los aretes, la bolsa de limosna y las cenizas del yogui. ¿Qué hace Guru Nanak allí con esos objetos?
options: obliga a los sijs a llevarlos en la oración del alba
los permite solo a los sijs que dejan su hogar
los nombra como atuendo de los cinco amados
hace de cada uno una virtud, como el contento
es.why: La pauri 28 dice: haz del contentamiento tus aretes, de la modestia tu bolsa de limosna, de la meditación tus cenizas, y de la humanidad tu orden; vence la mente y vencerás el mundo. Los Gurus vivieron como cabezas de familia.

stem: In Pauri 34 of Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7), Guru Nanak calls the earth a dharamsaal. What does that picture say the earth is?
options: a prison the soul must break out of
a home set up for right action
a waiting room before the next realm
a marketplace where all is sold
why: Pauri 34: tis vich dharatee thaap rakhee dharam saal, amid nights, seasons, air, water and fire, the earth is set as a house for dharma, where each is weighed by their own deeds. This is Dharam Khand, the first realm.
source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7 (Japji Sahib, pauri 34)

es.stem: En la pauri 34 del Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7), Guru Nanak llama a la tierra dharamsaal. ¿Qué dice esa imagen que es la tierra?
options: una prisión de la que el alma debe huir
un hogar dispuesto para el obrar recto
una sala de espera antes del otro reino
un mercado donde todo se vende
es.why: Pauri 34: tis vich dharatee thaap rakhee dharam saal, en medio de noches, estaciones, aire, agua y fuego, la tierra está puesta como casa del dharma, donde cada quien es pesado por sus propios actos. Es Dharam Khand, el primer reino.

stem: In Pauri 23 of Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5), Guru Nanak compares kings with mountains of wealth to an ant. What is the comparison, and what point does it make?
why: Pauri 23: kings and emperors with ocean-wide realms and mountains of wealth are not equal to an ant (keeRee) that does not forget the One in its mind. Remembrance (simran), not wealth or power, is what weighs.
source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5 (Japji Sahib, pauri 23)

rubric.point: says the kings, for all their wealth and kingdoms, are not equal to (do not measure up to) the ant. saying the ant is simply 'small but hardworking' does not count.
says the ant's worth comes from not forgetting the One in its heart or mind: remembrance, simran, keeping the Name. 'humility' alone is partly met.
mentions the stanza's other picture, rivers pouring into the ocean without knowing its size, or that praise cannot grasp how great the One is.

es.stem: En la pauri 23 del Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5), Guru Nanak compara a reyes con montañas de riqueza con una hormiga. ¿Cuál es la comparación y qué quiere mostrar?
es.why: Pauri 23: reyes y emperadores con reinos como océanos y riquezas como montañas no igualan a una hormiga (keeRee) que no olvida al Uno en su mente. Lo que pesa es el recuerdo (simran), no la riqueza ni el poder.

stem: Pauris 34 to 37 of Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7-8) describe five khands, or realms. Name them in order, and say who dwells in the last one.
why: Japji Sahib 34-37 names Dharam Khand (right action), Gian Khand (knowledge), Saram Khand (effort, or beauty and humility, by other readings), Karam Khand (grace) and Sach Khand (truth), where the Formless One, Nirankar, dwells and beholds creation.
source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7-8 (Japji Sahib, pauris 34-37)

rubric.point: names the five realms in order: Dharam Khand, Gian Khand, Saram Khand, Karam Khand, Sach Khand. four of five in the right order is partly met; English glosses (duty or right action, knowledge, effort, grace, truth) count as names.
says the Formless One (Nirankar, God) dwells in Sach Khand, the realm of truth. saying 'the saints' alone is partly met.
gives a sense of any realm: earth as the house of dharma, knowledge blazing, the mind shaped in Saram Khand (read as effort, or as beauty or humility), the mighty in spirit in Karam Khand.

es.stem: Las pauris 34 a 37 del Japji Sahib (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7-8) describen cinco khands, o reinos. Nómbralos en orden y di quién habita en el último.
es.why: Japji Sahib 34-37 nombra Dharam Khand (el obrar recto), Gian Khand (el conocimiento), Saram Khand (el esfuerzo, o la belleza y la humildad, según otras lecturas), Karam Khand (la gracia) y Sach Khand (la verdad), donde habita el Sin Forma, Nirankar, contemplando la creación.
